card.name: Cheoyongmu
card.tagline: A majestic five-person court dance from Korea designed to dispel evil spirits.
card.profile: Cheoyongmu is the oldest surviving Korean court dance, originating from the Unified Silla period. It features five dancers wearing distinct colored costumes representing the cardinal directions and the center. The dance serves both as a ritual to drive away evil spirits and a majestic display of traditional Korean court artistry.
card.insight: Danced by five men in masks of light wine-color, Cheoyongmu uses the philosophy of the Five Elements to transform a mythic exorcism of a smallpox spirit into a stately, vigorous performance of royal protection.
card.profile_long: Cheoyongmu is a storied Korean court dance rooted in the legend of Cheoyong, the son of the Dragon King Yongwang. According to tradition, Cheoyong saved his wife from a smallpox spirit by using dance and music to drive the entity away. This narrative evolved into a formal court performance, historically used during New Year’s Eve exorcism rites and royal banquets to ensure tranquility and good fortune. From the Silla period through the Goryeo dynasty, the dance was performed by a single dancer, but it eventually transitioned into a five-person performance during the Joseon era. The dancers are clad in white, blue, black, red, and yellow, symbolizing the four cardinal directions and the center, reflecting the Confucian theory of the Five Elements. Their attire is highly specific: they wear light wine-colored masks with white teeth, tin earrings, necklaces of lead beads, and black hats adorned with two peony blossoms and seven peaches—items believed to ward off malevolent forces. The movement style is characterized by majesty and vigor, shifting through various tempos and styles of music, which are punctuated by lyrical song recitations. Beyond the dance itself, the tradition encompasses the craftsmanship of mask-making and the folk belief that placing an image of Cheoyong on a house gate could repel disease. Though the dance faced a temporary disappearance following the 1910 annexation treaty, it was revived in the 1920s and remains a vital part of Korean cultural heritage, recognized by UNESCO in 2009.

sections.how_it_is_danced: The dance is performed by five men who move with stateliness and vigor. The performance is punctuated by lyrical song recitations and varies in tempo and style.
sections.music_and_instruments: The music includes lyrical song recitations and varies in style and tempo to accompany the dancers' movements.
sections.costume_and_setting: Dancers wear costumes in yellow, red, blue, white, and black. They don light wine-colored masks with white teeth, tin earrings, lead bead necklaces, and black hats decorated with two peony blossoms and seven peaches.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Originally a ritual to drive off evil spirits and smallpox, it was performed at royal banquets and New Year's Eve exorcisms to promote good fortune and tranquility.
sections.lineage: Derived from the legend of Cheoyong, son of the Dragon King Yongwang.
